research_questions: RQ-01: What are the available mechanisms for profile-specific seed data in Spring Boot 3 + Flyway?
RQ-02: How do Flyway repeatable migrations interact with versioned migrations and Spring profile-scoped locations?
RQ-03: What is the best idempotency strategy for seed data in a partitioned PostgreSQL schema?
RQ-04: How to write partition-safe INSERTs that work regardless of which month the seed runs?

findings.question: RQ-01
findings.title: Three viable mechanisms for profile-scoped seed data
findings.summary: Spring Boot 3 + Flyway offers three approaches: (A) Flyway repeatable migrations with profile-scoped spring.flyway.locations, (B) Spring ApplicationRunner with @Profile annotation, (C) spring.sql.init.data-locations. Option A is recommended by Flyway documentation for environment-specific data. Option C is discouraged by Spring when Flyway is active.

option_a.name: Flyway Repeatable Migration (R__ prefix)
option_a.mechanism: spring.flyway.locations adds a second directory only in the target profile. Files with R__ prefix run after all V* migrations. Re-run on checksum change.
pros: Native Flyway mechanism — zero custom code
Runs before application context (JPA validation succeeds)
Profile isolation via spring.flyway.locations (additive per profile)
Pure SQL — no Java code, no compile-time coupling
Checksum tracking — Flyway detects changes and re-applies
cons: SQL must be kept in sync with schema changes manually
Repeatable migrations lack version ordering (alphabetical by description)
option_a.spring_boot_docs_ref: Spring Boot 3.3.x — Flyway auto-configuration honors spring.flyway.locations property per active profile

option_b.name: Spring ApplicationRunner with @Profile("dev")
option_b.mechanism: @Component @Profile("dev") class DevSeedRunner implements ApplicationRunner. Uses JPA repositories to insert entities programmatically.
pros: Auto-adapts to entity refactors at compile time
Can build complex object graphs with builders
cons: Runs after full Spring context initialization (slower startup)
Requires @Order to ensure Flyway completes first
Mixes data seeding concern with application startup
Must handle Hibernate managed lifecycle (flush, detach, etc.)
Execution results partition routing depends on JPA configuration

option_c.name: spring.sql.init.data-locations
option_c.mechanism: Spring's native SQL initialization via spring.sql.init.mode=always and spring.sql.init.data-locations=classpath:data-dev.sql
cons: Spring documentation explicitly warns against using with Flyway (ordering not guaranteed)
No checksum tracking — re-runs on every startup unless gated
Does not participate in Flyway's migration lifecycle
option_c.spring_boot_docs_ref: Spring Boot docs: 'We don't recommend using multiple data source initialization technologies' — refers to mixing sql.init with Flyway

findings.question: RQ-02
findings.title: Flyway repeatable migration execution semantics
findings.summary: Flyway executes all pending versioned (V*) migrations in version order, THEN all pending repeatable (R__) migrations in alphabetical order by description. A repeatable migration is 'pending' when its checksum differs from the last recorded execution. This guarantees schema is fully current before seed data runs.

details.execution_order: V1 → V2 → V3 → V4 → V5 → R__dev_sample_data
details.re_run_trigger: Checksum change (any edit to the SQL file content)
details.profile_scoping: spring.flyway.locations is a list. The dev profile overrides it to include both classpath:db/migration (versioned) and classpath:db/seed/dev (repeatable seed). Other profiles only see classpath:db/migration.
details.important_note: When the dev profile OVERRIDES spring.flyway.locations, it must INCLUDE the base migration path. Otherwise, versioned migrations won't run. The override replaces, not appends.

findings.question: RQ-03
findings.title: Idempotency strategies for seed data
findings.summary: Three approaches: (1) DELETE-then-INSERT in a transaction (clean slate), (2) INSERT ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING (additive), (3) UPSERT ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE (replace). For ephemeral Zonky databases, option 1 is simplest and cleanest. For persistent databases, option 2 or 3 is safer.

strategy_1_clean_slate.sql_pattern: BEGIN; DELETE FROM child_tables; DELETE FROM parent_tables; INSERT INTO parent_tables ...; INSERT INTO child_tables ...; COMMIT;
pros: Guarantees exact expected state on every startup
Simplest to reason about — no conditional logic
DELETE order respects FK (children first, then parents)
cons: Destroys any user-created data in the dev database
Acceptable because Zonky database is ephemeral
strategy_1_clean_slate.use_when: Ephemeral database (Zonky) — every bootRun gets a fresh DB anyway

strategy_2_additive.sql_pattern: INSERT INTO ... ON CONFLICT (pk) DO NOTHING;
pros: Preserves user-created data alongside seed data
cons: Does not update existing seed rows if seed data changes
Seed modifications only visible after manual DELETE
strategy_2_additive.use_when: Persistent database where user data coexists with seed data

strategy_3_upsert.sql_pattern: INSERT INTO ... ON CONFLICT (pk) DO UPDATE SET col1=EXCLUDED.col1, ...;
pros: Updates seed data while preserving user-created data
cons: Most verbose SQL — every column listed in SET
strategy_3_upsert.use_when: Persistent shared dev database with evolving seed data

findings.recommendation: Strategy 2 (INSERT ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING) — works for both ephemeral Zonky and hypothetical persistent Postgres. Avoids destructive DELETEs while keeping SQL simple.

findings.question: RQ-04
findings.title: Partition-safe timestamp generation in SQL
findings.summary: Use date_trunc('month', CURRENT_TIMESTAMP) as the anchor for current-month data and subtract INTERVAL '1 month' for previous month. Adding random offsets within the month creates realistic temporal distribution. PartitionScheduler.bootstrap() creates partitions for current + 2 months on ApplicationReadyEvent, which runs AFTER Flyway — but V1 bootstraps 2026_04 and 2026_05 inline, so the seed SQL can safely target any month from April 2026 forward.

details.safe_range: From date_trunc('month', CURRENT_TIMESTAMP) TO date_trunc('month', CURRENT_TIMESTAMP) + INTERVAL '1 month'
details.previous_month_note: Previous month partitions exist only if PartitionScheduler.bootstrap() has run (ApplicationReadyEvent). Since Flyway runs BEFORE ApplicationReadyEvent, the seed SQL cannot reliably insert into 'last month' — the partition may not exist yet. HOWEVER, V1__init.sql hardcodes 2026_04 and 2026_05 partitions, and bootstrap() creates current + 2 months. So if today is April 2026 or later and bootstrap has run in any prior startup, the partition exists.
details.safe_approach: Only seed execution_results for the CURRENT month. The seed SQL runs after V1 (which creates 2026_04 and 2026_05) but before bootstrap(). To avoid partition-not-found errors, constrain all started_at values to fall within V1's hardcoded partitions OR use current-month only.
details.dynamic_approach: Use generate_series + CURRENT_TIMESTAMP to distribute data across the most recent 30 days, which naturally falls within the current-month partition. For multi-month spread, the PartitionScheduler.bootstrap() on ApplicationReadyEvent ensures current + 2 future months exist — so after first startup, the seed can target a wider range on subsequent runs.
details.recommended_pattern: Seed for current month only (safe on first run). PartitionScheduler.bootstrap() will create additional partitions, and the R__ migration re-runs on checksum change — so updating the seed later is trivial.

findings.question: RQ-01
findings.title: Existing precedent: V3__check_templates_seed.sql
findings.summary: The project already seeds data via Flyway. V3 creates check_templates and inserts 7 rows in a versioned migration. This establishes the pattern of using Flyway for data population. The difference: V3 is versioned (runs once, all profiles) while our seed should be repeatable (dev-only, re-runs on change).

details.pattern_in_v3: CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS + INSERT with static string PKs in a versioned migration
details.difference: V3 seeds reference data needed in ALL environments (templates). Dev seed is environment-specific.
details.alignment: Using Flyway for both schema AND data population is an established pattern in this codebase.

findings.question: RQ-03
findings.title: Trigger interaction with seed data
findings.summary: V1 defines two triggers: (1) update_updated_at_column (BEFORE UPDATE) and (2) update_check_status_from_execution (AFTER INSERT on execution_results). When seeding execution_results, trigger (2) will fire and propagate status + last_execution_at to the parent check. This means: insert execution_results AFTER checks, and the final execution_result for each check should have the desired 'current' status.

details.implication: The order of execution_results inserts matters. The LAST inserted result per check_id determines the check's visible status via the trigger.
details.strategy: Insert execution_results sorted by started_at ASC within each check_id. The last row (most recent) propagates the desired current status to the check.
details.bonus: No need to manually SET checks.status — the trigger handles it. INSERT checks with status='PENDING' and let execution_results trigger update it.
